title: American Oil Refiners Post Record Profits as Wars Squeeze Global Fuel Supplies
excerpt: Valero, Marathon and Phillips 66 are on track for record third-quarter earnings as the Iran war, Middle East refinery damage and Ukrainian strikes on Russia drive diesel margins to historic highs.
body:
• Valero, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 are projected to top their near-record Q2 profits this quarter — JPMorgan estimates Valero's pretax earnings at $8.95 billion, up 50% quarter-on-quarter.
  • Eight U.S. refiners are expected to earn $32.4 billion combined in the two quarters since the Middle East war began, up from $6.8 billion a year earlier (Finimize).
  • Record diesel "crack spreads" are driving the windfall — the Iran war, damaged Middle East refineries, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian plants and China's export pullback have left the U.S. as the world's last major fuel supplier.
  • What it means for you: diesel recently averaged a record $6.53 a gallon, feeding into groceries, freight and airfares; export-ban or windfall-tax talk is growing ahead of the midterms.

America's largest independent oil refiners are heading into the third quarter of 2026 with profits that Wall Street analysts say could set records — and the windfall is being driven not by anything they did, but by wars that have knocked out much of the rest of the world's fuel-making capacity.

Valero Energy, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 all reported their strongest quarterly profits since the start of the Ukraine war in the second quarter. Now analysts project the third quarter will be bigger still, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal.

Profits measured in the billions

JPMorgan analysts project Valero could print $8.95 billion in pretax earnings in the third quarter, up 50% from the previous three-month period and 24% higher than its previous quarterly record set in mid-2022, the Journal reported. Piper Sandler forecasts Marathon's per-share earnings will rise more than sevenfold from the same period last year, while Phillips 66's refining earnings are expected to eclipse its past record.

https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2108417852428394626

The scale of the boom extends across the sector. Eight publicly listed U.S. refiners are expected to make $32.4 billion combined in the two quarters since the Middle East war began, up from just $6.8 billion for the same period a year earlier, according to Finimize. The Financial Times put the figure higher still: revenues of $325.5 billion across the group, versus $242.9 billion a year earlier.

"Great for refiners… and not really anyone else."

— Charlie Pullan, analyst at Finimize

The crack spread explained

The windfall comes from the "crack spread" — the gap between the price of crude oil and the price of the fuels made from it. Crude has risen, but refined fuels have risen far faster, and refiners collect the difference on every gallon.

The WTI 3-2-1 crack spread has traded in the high-$50s to mid-$60s per barrel, with diesel margins near levels last seen during the 2022 energy crisis, according to Rystad Energy analyst Arne Skjæveland.

How wars reshaped the world's fuel map

Three sets of disruptions collided to produce the tightest fuel market in years. A resurgent Iran war has crippled refineries across the Middle East; Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked offline roughly a third of Russia's refining capacity, forcing Moscow to restrict fuel shipments through February; and China has sharply pulled back on fuel exports, partly because it is receiving less crude from the Middle East.

That has effectively left the United States as the world's last major fuel supplier. U.S. refinery output hit a five-year high of 17.4 million barrels a day in August and diesel exports reached a record 1.9 million barrels a day.

The price at the pump — and in the grocery aisle

For American households, the windfall shows up as record prices. Average U.S. diesel hit $6.53 a gallon, rippling into the cost of freight, groceries, lumber and airfares — trucks and ships run on diesel, planes on jet fuel — which can push wider inflation higher.

The politics are heating up ahead of the November midterm elections. Rep. Tim Burchett (R., Tenn.) has introduced a bill to ban fuel exports, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) said he was open to the idea, according to the Journal. A U.S. export ban would likely send prices for the rest of the world soaring — India has already imposed an export tax on diesel and gasoline. Trump, who campaigned on cheap energy, has blasted big oil for wringing cash out of American gas pumps; the industry counters that prices cannot fall until global flows recover and damaged Middle East refineries are rebuilt.

What to watch next

The three U.S. refiners are scheduled to report results in late October and early November. The larger question is how long the windfall lasts: energy analysts expect markets to remain tight through the end of 2027. But the boom carries exit risk — if diplomacy ends the Iran war, prices could collapse as oil floods back into the market. For NRIs, the direct effect is twofold: record fuel costs feed into everyday inflation in the U.S., while surging refinery stocks have been among the market's best performers — Valero, Marathon and Phillips 66 delivered average stock returns above 52% last quarter.
